name: Amira Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an underground loader at Kestrel Deep, a copper mine, and I fly in and out, two weeks on and two weeks off. My day is mucking ore from the draw points and tramming it to the ore pass, about 800 metres down. I love the focus of it, the way you feel the bucket bite. What wears me out is the heat at the bottom levels and the flights home every second Thursday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tomás teaches primary school in the city, so he's home when I'm not, which is the hard part. I bought a one-bedroom flat when I was twenty-four and I rent it out, and we've got about eight months of savings on top. I'm a union delegate's backup on my crew, and I'm one of four women on our roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and I'd be glad the hype didn't wreck anyone's job. I'd probably post something about how the money went into chatbots instead of ventilation at the bottom levels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it changes almost nothing. My work is hands on, and the bit of AI I use is for emails to the body corporate about the flat. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the roster and keep renting the flat. I'd still do the tele-remote loader course next year because the company's offering it free. And keep pushing for better heat breaks through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The only thing that bugs me is the flying, not the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the flying cost you at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás and I miss birthdays and the odd wedding, and we talk about it. We've said two more years of fly-in fly-out, then I find a mine near the city. That plan doesn't need AI to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do the tele-remote course if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's free and two of the guys on C crew already did it and liked it. Once a few people I trust try something, I'll try it. I don't go first, but I don't go last either.

say: I'd say I'm **glad the hype** didn't wreck anyone's job.
I'd complain that money went to **chatbots instead of ventilation** at the bottom levels.
think: My work is **hands-on**, so plateau AI changes almost nothing for me.
The only AI I use is for **emails** about my rental flat.
do: Keep the **two-weeks-on roster** and keep renting out the flat.
Take the free **tele-remote loader course** next year.
Push for better **heat breaks** at the bottom levels through the union.
feel: **Calm**, with the **fly-in fly-out** strain the only real ache.
S0.quote: Once a few people I trust try something, I'll try it. I don't go first, but I don't go last either.
fieldNote: Her main existing strain is **fly-in fly-out** time away from her partner, not money.
A rental flat plus eight months' savings make her one of the **most secure** on her crew.
She describes her own **adoption style** precisely: follow trusted peers, never lead.

steps.text: Keep working the two-weeks-on loader roster
Take the company's free tele-remote loader course
Push the union for longer heat breaks underground

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a say in how this gets rolled out, full stop. Planning and scheduling going to software means fewer people in the office and more pressure on us. I'd raise it at the next union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd watch the planning office shrink first. Underground, robots are slow because the conditions are rough. But tele-remote loading already exists, so my seat is on borrowed time, just a long loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tele-remote course for sure and get on the list for the control room shifts. I'd probably use the AI tools more, to read the new safety procedures quicker. And I'd keep the flat, it's my backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel it creeping, but I'm not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the planning office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya does our short-term schedules and she's brilliant, but that's exactly what the software's after. She's already asked me about the loader course. I'd tell her to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a control room job mean no more flying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Some mines run their loaders from a room in the city, which would be a dream for Tomás and me. A control room in the city would fix my fly-in fly-out problem and my robot problem at once.

say: I'd say **workers need a say** in how planning software gets rolled out.
I'd raise **pressure on crews** at the next union meeting.
think: The **planning office** shrinks first; underground robots come slower.
Tele-remote loading already exists, so my **seat** is on **borrowed time**.
do: Finish the **tele-remote course** and join the list for control room shifts.
Use **AI tools** more to read new safety procedures faster.
Keep the **rental flat** as a backup income.
feel: **Uneasy**, feeling the change creep but not panicking.
S1.quote: A control room in the city would fix my fly-in fly-out problem and my robot problem at once.
fieldNote: She sees a possible **upside**: remote work from the city would end the flying.
Her worry goes first to **Priya**, a planner whose tasks match what the software targets.
Steady adopter: she moves because **peers have proven** the course, not because she leads.

steps.text: Finish the tele-remote course and apply for control room shifts
Use AI tools to read new safety procedures
Keep renting out the flat as backup income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public money and rules, now, not after it hits. Pay people while they retrain and keep unions at the table. I'd be marching, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of the loader by 2031, and the control room jobs will be a tenth of the seats. Tomás's school won't vanish, but they'll cut staff once AI marks and plans lessons. Both our incomes would be wobbling at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd go hard at the control room roles before they fill up, using the course I'd have done. I'd keep renting the flat and freeze any spending on holidays. If that failed, I'd look at maintenance on the robots, because somebody still has to fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be the one awake at the camp at 2 a.m. scrolling job boards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Bali trip we've been saving for. Then the new car. I wouldn't touch the flat, because the rent from the flat is the one thing a robot can't take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd march. Would you also put your hand up for the control room early, ahead of others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the contradiction, isn't it. I'd fight for everyone and still grab my seat. I'd feel bad about it, but I've got eight months saved and not eight years.

say: I'd call for **public money and rules** before AGI hits.
I'd say pay people **while they retrain** and keep unions at the table.
think: I'm out of the **loader by 2031**, with control room seats about a tenth.
My partner's **teaching job** could shrink too, so both incomes wobble together.
do: Apply for **control room roles** straight away, before they fill up.
Cancel the **Bali trip** and the new car, but keep the flat.
Train in **robot maintenance** if the control room bid fails.
feel: **Alarmed**, picturing **2 a.m.** job-board scrolling at the camp.
S2.quote: The rent from the flat is the one thing a robot can't take.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the loader job**, and her partner's income may shrink as well.
She names her own **contradiction**: marching for everyone while grabbing her own seat.
The **three-year robot gap** is her window to get into the control room first.

steps.text: Apply for tele-remote control room roles straight away
Cancel the Bali trip and the new car purchase
Train in robot maintenance if the control room bid fails
March for public retraining pay with the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing, but I'd say we've got time to do this fairly, so let's not waste it. I'd want a retraining fund paid for by the mining companies. That would be my line at the pub and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit more breathing room. I'd be thirty-two when the office side changes and thirty-five when the robots take the loaders. That's enough time to get a second qualification done properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a certificate in electrical and instrumentation, the people who look after the sensors. I'd do it on my off-swings. Keep the flat, keep saving, and plan to move off the fly-in roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frantic. It's like seeing a storm on the radar, you've got time to get the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you talked to Tomás about this kind of thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. He thinks I'm too calm about it and I think he's too worried. We'd sit down and set a date to stop fly-in fly-out, probably the year the AGI news is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical and instrumentation rather than the control room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the control room is a few seats and the sensors are everywhere. Every robot needs somebody to calibrate it. I'd rather be the person the robots need than the person they replace.

say: I'd say there's **time** to do this **fairly**, so don't waste it.
I'd push for a **retraining fund** paid for by mining companies.
think: Five years gives me **breathing room** before robots take the loaders at thirty-five.
That's enough time for a **second qualification** done properly.
do: Start an **electrical and instrumentation** certificate on my off-swings in year one.
Keep the **rental flat** and keep saving.
Set a date with my partner to **stop fly-in fly-out**.
feel: **Anxious** but not frantic, like watching a **storm on radar**.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the person the robots need than the person they replace.
fieldNote: Five years turns her **alarm** into a **plan**, but she still expects the loader job to go.
She chooses **sensors** over the **control room** because there are more of those jobs.
Her partner worries more than she does, a **reverse** she points out herself.

steps.text: Start an electrical and instrumentation certificate on off-swings
Set a date with Tomás to stop flying in and out
Push for a company-funded retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so governments have no excuse to drop the ball. I'd want every mine to publish its automation plans early. Workers should see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, robots in 2039 means I'm forty. The scheduling and paperwork go digital in 2036, but I'd still be loading ore for a while after. My own job feels safe for now, just with an end date I'd be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the fly-in fly-out years we planned, then move to a mine near the city. Around 2030, once I've seen who's making it in the new jobs, I'd pick a course. I'd probably buy a second flat in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. Uneasy in the background, the way you think about a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until 2030 to choose a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in ten years half the new jobs everyone's talking about will disappear. I'd rather see which ones last. That's how I've always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a second flat mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a second rent coming in that doesn't depend on any mine. If my loader job goes in 2039, two rents and my partner's pay would cover the basics. That's my idea of safe.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, so governments have no excuse.
I'd want every mine to **publish** its **automation plans** early.
think: Robots in **2039** mean I'm forty, so my job feels safe for now.
Paperwork goes digital in 2036, but I'd **keep loading ore** a while after.
do: Finish the planned **fly-in fly-out years**, then move to a mine near the city.
Choose a **retraining course** around 2030 once the lasting jobs are clear.
Buy a **second flat** to add another rent.
feel: Pretty **settled**, with a background unease like thinking about a **pension**.
S4.quote: If my loader job goes in 2039, two rents and my partner's pay would cover the basics. That's my idea of safe.
fieldNote: With a decade's warning, her income looks **safe for now** and she plans in stages.
She deliberately **waits to see** which new jobs last before committing to a course.
Property is her **chosen buffer**: rents that don't depend on any mine.

steps.text: Move from fly-in fly-out to a mine near the city
Buy a second rental flat in the next few years
Pick a retraining course around 2030, once jobs settle

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit my job and Tomás's job close together, and the control room seats would go in a week. What would help is retraining that's paid, with a wage, not a voucher, and unions in the room deciding who goes where.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about women. My roster took fifteen years to get four women on it. If the old boys' club builds the new jobs, women like me will be pushed out again.

headlineQuote: My roster took fifteen years to get four women on it. If the old boys' club builds the new jobs, women like me will be pushed out again.
portrait: Amira is a 27-year-old **underground loader operator** who flies in and out to a copper mine.
She owns a **rental flat**, has eight months saved and lives with Tomás, a primary teacher.
A **steady adopter**, she follows trusted crewmates into new tools rather than leading.
She's calm in AI Plateau, uneasy in Steady Disruption and alarmed by **AGI by 2028**, when both incomes wobble.
With more time she plans an **instrumentation** certificate and a move closer to the city.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her loader job and her partner's teaching could shrink together.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining **with a wage**, not a voucher.
**Unions in the room** deciding who goes where, with women not pushed out.
